outcome: Nothing since 26 January 2024 settles the question: no amicable pair with opposite parity has been found or ruled out, and the latest sources I opened (the Chen–Tang–Zhan Lean formalization of 12 Jan 2026 and Pollack's preprint of 5 Oct 2026) still treat it as open. The one in-window preprint with an AI attribution (Pollack, attributed to ChatGPT Astra) bounds a different quantity, the number of integers up to x lying in amicable pairs, and does not touch parity.
problem_asks: (a) Whether there exists an amicable pair: two distinct positive integers m and n, each equal to the sum of the proper divisors of the other. (b) Whether such a pair can have opposite parity, that is one member odd and the other even. The question is one of existence (yes or no). It asks for neither counts, bounds, nor a restricted form, and it places no condition on coprimality, size, or the shape of the pair.

events.remains: Existence of any opposite-parity amicable pair, and existence of a coprime one.

The comments field says the paper was submitted to the American Mathematical Monthly, which 'was not able to accept it since, amazingly enough, the same result was published by A. A. Gioia' in the Monthly in 1967.

events.what_happened: T. Yamada, 'On the divisibility of odd perfect numbers, quasiperfect numbers and amicable numbers by a high power of a prime', arXiv:1609.08795. Its §1 Theorem 1.3 concerns relatively prime amicable pairs of opposite parity (m even, n odd, σ(m)σ(n)=(m+n)², and mn = 2^α·p1^(2β1)···pt^(2βt), where each 2βi+1 is divisible by a prime from a fixed finite set P). It concludes that mn has a prime factor below a constant C1. The paper states that it is unknown whether a relatively prime amicable pair exists, or whether an opposite-parity amicable pair exists. Read via the ar5iv HTML summary; the PDF was unreadable.

events.remains: Existence of any opposite-parity pair; existence of a coprime pair; any pair whose product lies outside the stated shape.

events.what_happened: Z. Chen, H. Tang and J. Zhan (Shanghai Dianji University), 'Formalization of Amicable Numbers Theory', arXiv:2601.07444, v1 posted 12 Jan 2026; the arXiv page lists no later version. A Lean 4 formalization (2,076 lines and 139 theorems, by the paper's own count). Section 3.7.4 'Parity Constraints' gives Lean theorems OddMemberSquareTheorem and EvenMemberFormTheorem (Listing 19): for an opposite-parity pair, the odd member is a perfect square and the even member has the form 2^k·a² with k at least 1 and a odd. The paper says 'No odd-even amicable pair is currently known, so these constraints remain theoretical.' Section 2.3 lists open questions: all known pairs have both members even, and the existence of both-odd pairs is unresolved. Section 3.8 (Listing 24) defines OddOddAmicableConj as a conjecture.
events.delivers: Formal versions of the known conditional constraint on any opposite-parity pair, with the same content as Gioia–Vaidya 1967 and D'Abramo 2005. It restricts the shape of any such pair. It does not establish that a pair exists or that none does, and the paper keeps existence open.
events.remains: Existence of an opposite-parity amicable pair, which the paper itself does not resolve.

The arXiv abstract page gives v1 as 26 Dec 2025; one search snippet gives 30 Dec. A gcd divisible by 2 forces both members to be even, so the part of that class with gcd at least 2 lies inside the both-even case (my inference from arithmetic, not a claim of the paper). Whether the class includes gcd 1 (that is, 2^0) I could not determine from the abstract page.
events.direction: Not about the question. It characterizes a class, and gives no object.

events.what_happened: P. Pollack, 'Amicable numbers', arXiv:2610.05661, v1 posted 5 Oct 2026 (11 pages; comments field: 'expository article on AI-generated work'). It defines A(x), the number of integers up to x that lie in an amicable pair, and proves Theorem 1: as x tends to infinity, A(x) ≤ x L(x)^(−1/2+o(1)). The abstract says 'We report on a proof, found by ChatGPT Astra, that'. Section 1 has an unnumbered 'Statement of AI usage' subsection (see ai). The paper's text, as I read it, does not mention parity, odd or even members, or opposite-parity pairs.
events.delivers: An upper bound on A(x), the count of integers up to x lying in amicable pairs. This is a density count, which the problem does not name. It establishes nothing about parity.
events.remains: The whole parity question. The paper also says it cannot prove that A(x) tends to infinity, which is a separate open question about the number of amicable pairs.

disputes.summary: D'Abramo's 2005 arXiv paper restates the odd-square and even-form constraint that Gioia and Vaidya published in the American Mathematical Monthly in October 1967. D'Abramo reports that the Monthly declined his submission for that reason. The 1967 paper is the earlier claim of the constraint, and neither is an existence result.

summary: I ran 38 web searches and opened about two dozen pages. No event since 26 January 2024 settles, or restricts-to-settle, anything the problem names. Every source I opened still treats the question as open: Wikipedia (read through a summarizing fetch), ProofWiki, OEIS A265757 (census: no known pair has opposite parity), the Lean paper of Jan 2026, and Pollack's preprint of Oct 2026. Before 2024 the literature holds only constraints and restricted cases, which I recorded as events. Gioia–Vaidya (Monthly, 1967) shows that any opposite-parity pair would have an odd square as its odd member and a square or twice a square as its even member; D'Abramo (2005) restates this on arXiv and reports a priority dispute with the Monthly. Kanold (1953) gives the coprime shape (m,n)=(2M²,N²) with M and N odd, and a lower bound on distinct prime factors. Hagis (1970) gives size bounds for coprime opposite-parity pairs (mn > 10^121; m, n > 10^60) from an abstract I read only through a summary. Jaroma and Mitchell (2005) prove, by their title, that no Fibonacci or Lucas number is a member of an opposite-parity pair, which I could not verify because the note is paywalled. Yamada (2016) gives a conditional restriction (Theorem 1.3) for a special factorization shape. None of these is an existence or non-existence result, and each is a restricted or conditional case, so under the scope test they narrow the problem's shape rather than resolve it. Close calls: (1) whether the constraint theorems in the 2026 Lean formalization count as progress; I treat them as formal versions of known conditional results, and the paper itself keeps existence open. (2) whether Pollack's bound moves the amicable-number count; it does, but the problem asks about parity and that count is not the quantity named. (3) whether Mavaddat–Alikhani's gcd-power-of-two class is parity-restricted; it is if the class excludes gcd 1, and I could not check that. AI search: the only AI attribution I found on amicable numbers is Pollack's, which the author states is for Theorem 1 (a density bound, not parity). I searched for AI involvement in the parity question with lab names, Astra, AlphaEvolve, Erdős-problem reports, and Tao's AI-contributions wiki (described secondhand only), and found nothing on parity. The OpenAI Astra announcement of 1 Aug 2026 (press, forklog) lists eight results, none about amicable numbers or parity. The AlphaEvolve paper (arXiv:2511.02864) has no amicable or aliquot term in the roughly 290,000 characters of its HTML that I could read, but the fetch truncated before the paper's end. Dates are the first public written argument (arXiv v1 dates; the journal dates for 1953, 1967 and 1970 come from citations, so their month is given only where a citation gives one).
competing_reading: The strongest case for a larger view: taken together, the 1953 coprime structure, the 1967 constraint, the 1970 size bounds, the 2005 Fibonacci/Lucas case, the 2016 conditional restriction and the 2026 formalization pin any counterexample to a very narrow form (odd member a square, even member a square or twice a square, coprime case huge), which might be read as a substantial partial resolution. Under the scope test (§2.1) these narrow the shape of any pair that might exist and do not answer whether one does, and the problem asks only that. A second reading would count Pollack's 2026 bound as moving 'amicable numbers', since the subject of the problem is amicable numbers. The statement names parity, and the bound does not touch parity.
what_would_settle_it: Either an explicit opposite-parity amicable pair (which would settle existence), or a published proof that none exists. Short of that: the full texts of Gioia–Vaidya (1967) and Hagis (1970) to confirm their exact hypotheses, especially whether Hagis's bounds and Kanold's are restricted to coprime pairs; the full text of Jaroma–Mitchell (2005) to confirm what its non-existence covers; the full text of Yamada (2016) and whether it was published; the Lean repository's sorry status and which §3.7.4 theorems are proved; and a verbatim reading of Pollack's §1 'Statement of AI usage' from the PDF, since the quotations I have come from a summarizing fetch.

events.credibility_reason: The paper's text is internally inconsistent about whether the parity constraint theorems are proved or only stated, and sorry status is unverified; in any case it formalizes known 1967 results.

events.ai_basis: The proof of Theorem 1 was produced by ChatGPT Astra.

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether an opposite-parity amicable pair exists. No event exhibits one or proves none exists. The shape constraints (Kanold's structure result, Gioia–Vaidya, D'Abramo, Yamada) are conditional on such a pair existing and settle nothing, so they are none. Lower bounds on the size or complexity of coprime opposite-parity pairs (Kanold, Hagis) were answered bound; this was a close call between bound and none, but they are pre-snapshot and cannot affect the status. Jaroma–Mitchell settles a restricted class (pairs with a Fibonacci or Lucas member), so it is a case, also pre-snapshot. The OEIS parity census is instances. Of the post-snapshot events, the 2026 Lean paper formalizes known constraints (none). Mavaddat–Alikhani does not address parity (none). Pollack's AI-generated density bound answers a different question about amicable numbers, the count A(x), not parity (variant). Its ai_role is generated on the author's own statement, but that credit does not attach to the parity question.
judgement.doubts: The pre-snapshot journal papers were known only through citations. Their verification is marked digested because they appeared in journals of record, and the exact hypotheses of the Hagis and Kanold bounds were not confirmed. None of this affects the post-snapshot reading.
